title: Family rejects apology from London cop convicted in Indigenous woman's death
subtitle: The family of a woman who died in police custody four years ago rejected an apology issued Thursday by the London officer convicted in her death and criticized the courts for delaying his sentencing.
article: The family of a woman who died in police custody four years ago rejected an apology issued Thursday by the London officer convicted in her death and criticized the courts for delaying his sentencing.
Const. Nicholas Doering, 30, delivered an apology at the sentencing hearing for his role in the Sept. 7, 2016, death of Debra Chrisjohn, 39.

But Doering, who was found guilty of criminal negligence causing death and failing to provide the necessaries of life in November, won't find out for weeks if he's heading to jail after the judge in the case reserved her decision.
The Crown is seeking a sentence of 20 to 30 months, while the defence is pushing for probation and community service as part of a conditional sentence.
"I wanted once again to express how deeply sorry I am for the loss of your loved one," Doering said when asked whether he wished to address the court.

"I continue to struggle with reliving the reality for what occurred that day. While it doesn't compare to what they must be going through, I know that they lost a mother, a sister, a friend. So I just want to say I'm sorry again."

The apology, delivered over a video feed broadcast on YouTube, is the second Doering has publicly delivered to the family of Chrisjohn, who died in hospital after going into medical distress at the Elgin County OPP detachment.

Doering arrested the mother of 11 after she was found trying to get into vehicles in east London while high on crystal meth. He transferred Chrisjohn into OPP custody on an outstanding warrant, falsely telling two officers that she'd been medically cleared, court heard.

Following Thursday's hearing, the Chrisjohn family issued a statement opposing a conditional sentence and blasting the courts for delaying the sentencing, which was originally scheduled for March, but was delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic.
"Our family has waited too long for justice and I truly believe he is only sorry for what he did because now he is facing consequences," Chrisjohn's sister, Cindy, said of Doering in the statement.

"Those consequences should not include being allowed to remain comfortably inside his home. If he is allowed a conditional sentence, police will have zero incentive to change their actions in the future."
Defence lawyer Lucas O'Hara argued that a conditional sentence would be appropriate for his client, a first-time offender who is undergoing treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder.

"Police services have been put on notice across the country because of this conviction and Mr. Doering will have a criminal record going forward . . . that he'll have to deal with for the rest of his life."
Jailing Doering would put him at risk of COVID-19 and derail his mental health treatment, O'Hara said.

But Crown attorney Jason Nicol said the mitigating factors that O'Hara highlighted weren't exceptional enough to justify a conditional sentence, calling jail time "the only just and reasonable sentence."

"No one can deny that the fact that Ms. Chrisjohn died as a result of Const. Doering's criminal activity," Nicol said. "There has to be a denunciatory, punitive sentence that recognizes what he did and the consequences of what he did."
Justice Renee Pomerance will deliver her sentence on Sept. 21.
